products.name: Bloom Energy Server sold to utilities (the 'utility channel' Bernstein highlighted)
products.what_it_is: The same solid-oxide fuel-cell boxes Bloom sells to data centers, bought by an electric utility to add power to its grid instead of a single customer using them on site.
products.analogy: Like a bakery that has sold to one big restaurant chain and now starts supplying supermarkets too: same bread, a second kind of buyer.
products.buyers: Utilities planning capacity. Ameren's resource plan (released 2026-09-28) includes 500 MW of natural-gas fuel cells by 2030 (per Barclays and Bernstein notes, tier 3; Ameren document not opened). Virginia's 2026 Energy Plan names fuel cells as a near-term option (Bloom not named). AEP is a known earlier Bloom utility customer.
products.how_it_works: Natural gas reacts chemically (no burning) inside stacks of ceramic cells to make electricity. Units are modular and can be installed in months, versus years for a big new power plant or grid connection.
products.sales: Utility sales not disclosed separately. Proxy (labelled): Q2 2026 product revenue $935.4m of $1,065.4m total revenue; FY2026 revenue guidance $3.9-4.2bn.
products.stage: Shipping; utility orders are early-stage. Ameren's 500 MW is a plan to 2030, not a signed Bloom order (no Bloom-Ameren contract found).
products.size_for_company: not disclosed. Bernstein places the utility channel's revenue mostly in 2029-2035 (opinion).
products.competition: Gas turbines and engines (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Caterpillar), batteries, solar/wind plus storage, and other fuel-cell makers (FuelCell Energy).
products.why_investors_care: If utilities become regular buyers, Bloom depends less on a handful of data-center projects such as Oracle's Jupiter.
products.watch_next: Q3 2026 results (late October): any utility orders, backlog, and whether the 2026 outlook holds.
